title: Khalid ibn al-Walid
hookLine: the commander whose horsemen turned Uhud against the Muslims, later fighting for them

cards: Go back to the hillside at Uhud. The Muslims seem to be winning. The archers posted on a hill to guard the rear see the enemy running, leave their post, and come down for the spoils.
The Qur'an, in the surah called the Family of Imran, speaks of that moment: some wanted this world, and the tide turned. Who turned it?

The biographies name the man leading the Meccan horsemen, who saw the empty hill and rode around behind the Muslim lines: Khalid ibn al-Walid. Today: the man who broke the Muslims at Uhud, and what he did next.

teach.b: Uhud cost the Muslims dearly. Companions we have met on this road died there, Mus'ab with his short cloak among them.

Later, the biographies say, Khalid came to Medina to become Muslim. Picture that community the day he walked in: this is the man whose horsemen came around the hill. What does a community do with that?

teach.h: A SWORD OF GOD AT MU'TAH.
teach.b: At Mu'tah, the battle where Ja'far and the other appointed leaders fell one after another, Sahih al-Bukhari records the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, telling the people in Medina what had happened.
Zayd took the banner and fell. Ja'far took it and fell. Ibn Rawahah took it and fell.
Then the banner was taken by one of the swords of God, and God gave them a way through. That sword was Khalid. Tradition calls him Saifullah, the sword of God.
How does the man who broke the lines at Uhud become that? A report in Sahih Muslim gives the principle, through another Meccan who came over, Amr ibn al-As.

teach.h: ISLAM WIPES OUT WHAT CAME BEFORE.
teach.b: When Amr hesitated, afraid of his past, the Prophet told him that Islam wipes out what came before it. The past is not erased from history; Uhud still happened. But it is not held against the man who turned.
A community that believes people change can find its sword in its old enemy.

how: Muslims teach that accepting Islam wipes out what came before it, and the companions' stories, Khalid's among them, are told as examples of former opponents welcomed and trusted.

o: a war cry shouted as a battle began
a sword the Prophet carried into battle
the sword of God, the title given to Khalid

games.q: Khalid ibn al-Walid — tap the pairs.
p: left the hill for the spoils
where he took up the banner
told Islam wipes out what came before

s: Khalid fought for the Muslims at Uhud
he led the Meccan horsemen at Uhud; he became Muslim later.
the Prophet called Khalid one of the swords of God
after Mu'tah, in Bukhari: the banner was taken by one of the swords of God.
becoming Muslim meant Uhud was forgotten
Uhud still happened. what the hadith says is that it is not held against the one who turned.

games.q: you're one of the believers in Medina. Khalid, whose horsemen broke your lines at Uhud, arrives to become Muslim. what does the community do?
o: turn him away; Uhud is too fresh.
accept him, but never trust him with anything.
welcome him, and soon trust him with the banner.
games.why: he was welcomed, and at Mu'tah he took the banner. the Prophet called him one of the swords of God.

practice: Bring to mind someone you've filed under who they used to be: a cousin who was cruel in school, a coworker who once let you down, maybe yourself.
Ask honestly whether you've watched closely enough to know who they are now, and leave a door open without forgetting what happened. If you pray, you can ask good for that person by name.

wordCard.voice: Saifullah, the sword of God, the title given to Khalid ibn al-Walid after the same horsemen who broke the Muslims at Uhud carried their banner at Mu'tah. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the sword of God, the title tradition gives Khalid, from the Mu'tah report.

carryVoice: Your line: people change. Uhud still happened, and the door stayed open. That's day eight hundred forty-three.

sources.ref: Qur'an 3:152 (at Uhud some wanted this world, and the tide turned)
